collectionunit.notes: "Three sediment cores were collected using a hand-held D-section (or Russian) peat corer. Two cores (a 0.45-m core and a 0.95-m core) were taken from Wathumba (Fig. 2) and a 3.15-m core was collected from Moon Point (Fig. 3). These cores underwent detailed sedimentological, palynological and char- coal analysis to characterise the environmental history of the Moon Point and Wathumba patterned fen complexes."-Moss 2015

site.sitedescription: "Fraser Island has a subtropical maritime climate with warm, humid summers and dry, cool winters (Fig. 1). The summer-dominant precipitation is ,1274 mm per year, and temperatures range from a mean maximum high of 25.88C (highest monthly temperature is 29.48C in January and the lowest is 21.18C in July) and a mean maximum low of 18.88C (lowest mean monthly temperature is 14.38C in July and 22.48C in February). […] The key plant taxon comprising the patterned fen complexes is the peat-developing rush Empodisma minus (Wagstaff and Clarkson 2012), which generally forms the strings and base of the flarks. Other common taxa in the fens include Leptospermum liversidgei, Epacris microphylla, Sprengelia sprengelioides, Banksia robur, Gahnia sieberiana, Gleichenia dicarpa, Gleichenia mendellii and Hibbertia salicifolia. The fen water is highly acidic (pH of 4.3–4.8), with the underlying sediments consisting of very organic peats varying in depths of 1–3 m (generally deeper in the larger complexes). Fires occur within the patterned fen complexes and the key impacts seem to be a reduction in shrub cover (Fairfax et al. 2011). It has been suggested that the vertical-ascending E. minus roots protect the base of the fen from damage and prevent the ignition of the underlying peat (Fairfax et al. 2011). Currently, fire management within the Great Sandy National Park uses deliberate burning to promote biodiversity and reduce fire hazard, but there is scope to alter management strategies based on improved understanding of the region’s fire history, Indigenous knowledge and potential damaging impacts on key communities (e.g. the patterned fens) (EPA/QPWS 2005). Furthermore, there is evidence that the patterned fen complexes have been extremely stable for decades, with aerial photographs from 1958 and 2010 suggesting very little change in the structure of the pattern fen complex at Moon Point and Wathumba (Fairfax et al. 2011)." -Moss, 2015
